extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, reviewers, and students interested in scholarly peer review
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, procedures, formats, and responsibilities for reviewing and making editorial/funding decisions on academic manuscripts and proposals. Covers stages (desk evaluation, external review, revisions), reviewer selection, anonymity models, open/transparent review variants, and reforms like registered reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and justification of peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is the process of having a draft version of a researcher's methods and findings reviewed (usually anonymously) by experts in the same field to help editors decide whether work should be accepted, accepted with revisions, or rejected for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review encourages authors to meet accepted standards of their discipline and reduces dissemination of irrelevant findings, unwarranted claims, unacceptable interpretations, and personal views. It is generally considered necessary to academic quality, though it does not prevent publication of invalid research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of novelty and substantive contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: For both grant-funding and publication in a scholarly journal, it is normally a requirement that the subject is both novel and substantial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a common underlying standard influencing editorial and funding decisions and is used implicitly in desk evaluation and referee assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desk evaluation / desk rejection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor evaluates the manuscript to judge whether the paper will be passed on to journal referees; many articles receive a "desk reject."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (European Accounting Review): 1) fit for the journal's aims and scope, 2) sufficiency of paper content (literature review, methods, conclusions) and whether it makes a worthwhile contribution, 3) compliance with format and technical specifications. If 'no' to any, the manuscript may be desk rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: External review: referee selection and roles
rubrics_metrics.description: If not desk rejected, editors send the manuscript to referees chosen for their expertise and distance from the authors; typically one to three referees review the paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees evaluate the work, note weaknesses and suggestions for improvement, and return an evaluation and often an explicit recommendation. Referees' role is advisory; editors make final decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees' recommendation options (example: Nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees often choose among a set of recommended courses of action such as: unconditionally accept; accept if authors improve in certain ways; reject but encourage revision and invite resubmission; reject outright.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors typically consider these recommendations but are not strictly bound by them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling referee disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple referees disagree substantially, editors have several strategies: reject, instruct authors to address a particular reviewer's points, solicit additional reviews as tie-breakers, or invite authors to rebut criticisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors may convey communications between authors and referees to allow debate; multiple referees are not normally allowed to confer with each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to reviewers: best-practice rules (William Stafford Noble)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ten rules for responding to reviewers include: provide an overview then quote reviews; be polite and respectful; accept blame; make the response self-contained; respond to every point; use typography to help navigation; begin responses with direct answers; when possible do what reviewer asks; be clear about what changed; if necessary write the response twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These rules serve as practical guidance for authors preparing revision letters and responses to improve communication and increase chance of acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer selection criteria: expertise, distance, and conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors solicit reviewers who are experts in the manuscript's topic and ideally at some distance from authors; referees should inform editors of any conflicts of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are sometimes asked to name qualified referees or people to be excluded (with justification). Journals vary in how much author input they accept; exclusion may be used to avoid bias but can be controversial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest disclosure and management
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees are supposed to inform the editor of any conflict of interests; conflicting reviewers can be prohibited from reviewing or their comments interpreted with the reported conflict in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals and editors apply policies to disqualify or treat conflicted reviewers differently; management depends on severity (e.g., past collaborators vs mild professional connection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity models: single-blind, double-blind, and attributed review
rubrics_metrics.description: In anonymous (blind) peer review the reviewers' identities are kept from authors; in double-blind review authors' identities are also concealed from reviewers; attributed review reveals reviewers' identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double-blind is more common in social sciences and humanities; critics say anonymity often fails due to identifiable styles or methods. Choice of model aims to reduce bias but has trade-offs in implementation and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open peer review (open identities, open reports, open participation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open peer review encompasses modifications such as open identities (authors and reviewers know each other's identity), open reports (review reports published alongside the article), and open participation (wider community can contribute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These modifications aim to address perceived shortcomings of traditional review such as lack of transparency, lack of incentives, wastefulness, and bullying/harassment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Transparent peer review publishes the documents relating to the publication of the paper alongside the paper (initial reviewer report, authors' response, acceptance letter); reviewer names may still be anonymous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides readers with access to review history while retaining some anonymity if desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-publication and preprint (open pre-publication) review
rubrics_metrics.description: Manuscripts are often reviewed by colleagues before submission; uploading to preprint servers (ArXiv, bioRxiv, SSRN) allows open pre-publication peer review where anyone can comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages include speed and transparency and wider feedback; disadvantages include more papers presented publicly without guaranteed quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review and open peer commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: After publication, readers may send letters to the editor, post comments, or engage in open peer commentary where specialists' commentaries and authors' replies are published alongside the target paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External platforms (e.g., PubPeer) allow anonymous commenting and can pressure authors to respond; some journals formally consider post-publication reviews as part of editorial processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-blind peer review and registered reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Result-blind peer review hides or removes results/conclusions during review to reduce positivity/publication bias; registered reports (pre-accepted articles) review study rationale and methods before data collection and commit to publication regardless of outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two-stage models exist. Registered reports shift emphasis to research questions and methods, improve adherence to preregistration, and reduce incentives for 'fishing' or selective reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor authority and advisory role of referees
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision whether to publish ultimately lies with the editor-in-chief or editorial board; referees provide opinions and recommendations that editors use but are not strictly bound by.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors usually follow referees' advice but retain final judgment and may weigh referee comments against each other and their own assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial acceptance criteria (Elsevier editors' factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors that drive article acceptance include: delivering 'new insight into an important issue', usefulness to practitioners, advancing or proposing a new theory, raising new questions, appropriate methods and conclusions, presenting a good argument based on the literature, and telling a good story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criteria illustrate the mix of intellectual novelty, methodological soundness, relevance, and readability that editors seek.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees' evaluation content and confidential comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees' evaluations typically note weaknesses or problems and include suggestions for improvement; referees can also send 'for your eyes only' confidential comments to editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most referees' comments are eventually seen by authors, but confidential comments may be used to communicate sensitive concerns to editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal peer review (colleague/editorial pre-review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal peer review is having a colleague or in-house reviewer read a paper before external submission (or internal editorial review before external review).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal review can improve papers but may suffer from in-house bias and conflicts with institutional goals; it is recommended for authors with weak writing skills or to improve grant applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recruiting referees: incentives, workload, and crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: Picking reviewers typically falls to an editor; recruiting is challenged by unpaid effort, time costs, and a growing volume of submissions leading to a 'peer review crisis.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are usually unpaid because payment could create conflicts of interest; suggestions include formally rewarding reviewers academically to sustain the system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author involvement in reviewer selection and risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals allow authors to suggest reviewers or choose reviewers; authors can sometimes exclude certain reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author-suggested reviewers may speed reviews but can be abused (fake reviews) and has led to fraud in some journals; policies vary and some journals have removed the option after abuses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability and criticisms of anonymous peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional anonymous peer review has been criticized for lack of accountability, potential abuse by reviewers or editors, bias, and inconsistency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These criticisms motivate calls for open peer review, transparent review, reviewer-report publication, and other reforms to increase accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archiving data and methods for audit and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals and agencies maintain and archive scientific data and methods to enable replication or audit after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archiving supports post-publication verification and audit when the review process alone cannot guarantee reproducibility; it is used by organizations like Science, AGU, NIH, NSF.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of social media and informal channels in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media, blogs, and hashtags can enable informal, post-publication peer review by a wider community (example: #arseniclife controversy), allowing rapid critique and replication attempts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such channels can legitimize scientific critique and attract media attention; they illustrate how community scrutiny complements formal review but may lack gatekeeping for quality.
